source.title: Can Neural Nets Learn the Same Model Twice? Investigating Reproducibility and Double Descent from the Decision Boundary Perspective
source.authors: Gowthami Somepalli; Liam H. Fowl; Arpit Bansal; Ping Yeh-Chiang; Yehuda Dar; Richard Baraniuk; Micah Goldblum; T. Goldstein

record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly says it follows Nakkiran et al.'s experimental setting to replicate double descent, sweeping ResNet-18 width and measuring test error.
record.gate_note: The test-error values are presented in Figure 6 without numeric values in the text. The paper also measures fragmentation and decision-boundary reproducibility around the interpolation threshold. Results in Section 3 on optimizer comparisons, distillation, and architecture-dependent reproducibility are not double-descent test-error results; cited findings from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper follows Nakkiran et al.'s ResNet-18 width sweep on CIFAR-10, with 0% and 20% label noise, and reports test error against width (Fig. 6). That is the original method and measure for V1. The clean-versus-noisy contrast bears on V6's label-noise dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors replicate double descent with 20% label noise but not with clean labels. They link the peak to unstable, non-reproducible, fragmented decision regions near interpolation, matching linear-model variance theory. They argue this instability, not error regions around mislabeled points, mainly drives double descent. They also note the peak precedes zero training error, unlike in simple linear models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper says it follows Nakkiran et al.'s experimental setting for a ResNet-18 width sweep and replicates double descent. It studies CIFAR-10 test error alongside decision-boundary geometry, and specifies 4000 training epochs with Adam at learning rate 0.0001.
record.method_sensitivity: The test-error double-descent result is pronounced with 20% label noise and not strong enough to appear without label noise. Decision-boundary fragmentation and reproducibility also vary around the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Decision-region fragmentation peaks sharply at the interpolation threshold with label noise. A smaller peak near k=7 appears without label noise (Fig. 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near the interpolation threshold, neural decision regions fragment into many small class regions, most strongly under label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Decision-boundary reproducibility across seeds (Fig. 11) and data orderings (Fig. 18) is high in narrow and wide networks but dips at the interpolation threshold. The dip is much larger with label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model variance, measured as decision-boundary reproducibility, spikes at the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Median margins grow for k≥10, including for mislabeled points (Fig. 12). The authors read this as double descent being driven by unnecessary oscillations, not by error regions around mislabeled points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The second descent comes from vanishing boundary instability rather than from shrinking regions around mislabeled points.

record.problems: The test-error curves and quantitative fragmentation and reproducibility curves are reported as figures without numeric values in the text. The width sweep is for one architecture, ResNet-18, and no uncertainty estimates are reported for these outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No further directly relevant test-error conditions were reported in text or tables. Appendix Figure 16 shows training-error curves, but training error is not the test-error outcome named by the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: Architectures other than ResNet-18, datasets other than CIFAR-10, and noise levels other than 0% and 20%.
Any effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Multiple peaks, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Re-expressing complexity as an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Training error versus width with and without noise. With 20% noise, zero training error is reached at much higher k than the test-error peak (k≈10). This bears on where V1 places the peak.
Median margin versus width, with and without label noise, including for mislabeled points only.

record.verdict_notes: All test-error evidence is in figures only, with no uncertainty reported. Only one architecture (ResNet-18) is swept for double descent. The Section 3 architecture, optimizer and distillation results do not bear on any version. The reader's V6 verdicts relied on fragmentation and reproducibility rows. These are related constructs, so they were moved to fits_no_version. V6 is now judged only on the test-error noise contrast.

versions.untested_parts: Other deep-network architectures and settings beyond the tested ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 width sweep.
A sweep over training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
Double descent across multiple model classes as a general capacity curve.
A unified effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Whether multiple test-error peaks occur, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Re-expressing complexity in effective parameter counts and testing whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: ResNet-18, 20% label noise; peak location versus training fit
relationships.reason: Per the Appendix D text (Figs. 16–17, not in rows), the test-error peak at k≈10 precedes zero training error, which comes at much higher k. So the peak does not sit exactly where the model just fits the training set.
relationships.display_finding: With 20% label noise, test error peaked near k≈10, while zero training error required substantially larger k.
